files.lesson.md: --- order: 55 unit: scatter10 node: AC9M10ST03 n1 uses: ["AC9M7A05 n3", "AC9M9ST03 n1"] connection: arm-span title: Scatterplots summary: "A scatterplot turns each person into one dot, using two measurements: the first goes across and the second goes up. Plot a dot, read a dot, and see whether the dots sit near a line." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Is your arm span the same as your height? Measure a whole class and you get a lot of numbers. A picture can show them all at once." explainPicture: { ref: armspan.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Twelve students (made up). The dashed line is where height equals arm span. Tom's dot, arm span 150 and height 175, is the one above it on the left." } app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8450 url: http://127.0.0.1:8450/index.html readySelector: "#board" layout: full --- A class measured their height and their arm span, in centimetres. Each student gives two numbers, so each student can be one dot: the arm span goes across, the height goes up. The measurements in this lesson are made up. Have a guess where Tom's dot goes, then we'll plot the whole class. ## Predict: where is Tom's dot? ```step stage: predict insight: "Placing a dot for a student who is taller than their arm span shows whether students put the first number across and the second up, and whether they see the dashed line as 'the same'." check: type: predict q: "Tom's arm span is $150$ cm and his height is $175$ cm. The dashed line is where height equals arm span. Where is Tom's dot, with arm span across and height up?" options: - "Above the dashed line" - "On the dashed line" - "Below the dashed line" - "Nowhere: you can't plot two measurements in one dot" actual: "Above the dashed line. His arm span is 150, so the dot is 150 across. His height is 175, so it is 175 up. On the dashed line the two numbers are equal, and Tom's height is bigger, so he is above it." ``` Make a guess before you check. ## Run: one dot at a time ```step stage: run insight: "Each student is one dot: arm span across, height up. A dot above the dashed line means a student whose height is more than their arm span." try: { playground: board, starter: "armspan.yml#run", height: 600 } check: { type: board, text: "Drag $P$ to Tom's spot: arm span $150$, height $175$. Was your prediction right?", when: "x(P) = 150 and y(P) = 175" } ``` The purple dots are twelve students (made up). The dashed line is where height equals arm span. $P$ is one more student for you to place; the arrow buttons under the graph move it a step at a time. ## Investigate: reading and plotting ```step stage: investigate insight: "A scatterplot is read one dot at a time: across for the first variable, up for the second. Swapping the two puts every dot in the wrong place, and the dashed line helps check." tasks: - hint: ["For each student compare the two numbers: is the second one (height) bigger than the first (arm span)?", "A dot is on the line when the two numbers are equal."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Five students (made up) have these (arm span, height) pairs in cm: $(150, 155)$, $(160, 158)$, $(170, 170)$, $(175, 180)$, $(182, 179)$. Plot them on paper with the dashed line height = arm span. How many of the five dots are above the line?" steps: - ["$(150, 155)$: $155 > 150$", "height is bigger than arm span, so the dot is above the line"] - ["$(175, 180)$: $180 > 175$", "height is bigger again, so this dot is above too"] - ["$(160, 158)$ and $(182, 179)$: height is smaller", "these two dots are below the line"] - ["$(170, 170)$: the numbers are equal", "this dot is on the line, so it is not above it"] - ["$2$ dots are above the line", "count the dots above"] answer: "2" answerLabel: "Dots above the line" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["3", "One of the five is on the line, not above it: (170, 170) has equal numbers."] - ["1", "Two dots have a height bigger than the arm span: (150, 155) and (175, 180)."] criteria: - "I put the arm span across and the height up for every dot." - "I compared the two numbers of each student, not just the look of the dots." - "I counted a dot on the line as not above it." explain: "(150, 155) and (175, 180) are above, (160, 158) and (182, 179) are below, and (170, 170) is on the line. So 2 are above." - picture: { ref: armspan.yml#plain, caption: "Arm span across and height up, 12 students (made up). The dashed line is height = arm span." } check: type: question q: "Which student is the tallest? Read the highest dot across, then up." options: ["Arm span $181$ cm, height $183$ cm", "Arm span $183$ cm, height $181$ cm", "Arm span $176$ cm, height $172$ cm", "Arm span $152$ cm, height $150$ cm"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That swaps the two. The arm span is across the bottom, so it is read first: 181 across, then 183 up.", "That dot is lower and further left. The highest dot is at the top right.", "That dot is the lowest one, at the bottom left."] explain: "The highest dot is far to the right and at the top: 181 across and 183 up." - picture: { ref: armspan.yml#plain, caption: "The same twelve students." } check: type: number q: "How many of the 12 dots are above the dashed line? (Those students are taller than their arm span.)" answer: 6 feedback: - [12, "That is every student. Some dots are below the line."] - [5, "Count again, one dot at a time, left to right: six are above."] explain: "Six dots are above the line (heights 157, 163, 166, 171, 175, 183) and six are below it." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#mia" text: "Mia plots Tom's dot. Click the line where her reasoning goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: scatter-axes-swapped explain: "Line 3: she put the bigger number across because it is bigger. The first measurement named, arm span (150), goes across, and the second, height (175), goes up. That puts Tom above the line, not below it." ``` ### Five students Here is how to plot one dot, then compare it with the dashed line. ```worked \text{arm span } 172, \text{ height } 169 :: One student gives two numbers. The first, arm span, goes across. \text{across to } 172 :: Start at the corner and move right to 172 on the arm span axis. \text{up to } 169 :: From there move up to 169 on the height axis and mark the dot. 169 < 172 :: On the dashed line, height equals arm span. Here the height is smaller, so the dot is below the line. ``` Now try five students on paper first, with the worked example beside you. ### Reading the tallest ### Counting above the line ### Find the mistake Read Mia's working. Which line puts the numbers the wrong way round? ## Modify: when dots share or break the pattern ```step stage: modify insight: "Two students can share a number, and a slip in the units shows at once on a plot. Dragging P to these cases shows what a scatterplot does with them." try: { playground: board, starter: "armspan.yml#tied", height: 600 } tasks: - hint: ["One of the purple dots already has arm span 160 cm. Put $P$ at the same arm span but a different height.", "Arm span is across, so keep 160 across and move up to 165."] check: { type: board, text: "Plot a new student with arm span $160$ cm and height $165$ cm. A purple student already has arm span $160$ cm.", when: "x(P) = 160 and y(P) = 165" } - check: type: question q: "Two students have the same arm span but different heights. What does the scatterplot show?" options: ["Two dots at the same place across, one above the other", "One dot, because the arm span is the same", "Two dots at the same height, side by side", "The plot can't show it"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Each student is still their own dot. The heights are different, so the dots are at different places up the side.", "Side by side would mean the same height and different arm spans.", "A scatterplot shows any pair of numbers, including two with the same first number."] explain: "Both dots are 160 across. One is 163 up and the other is 165 up, so one sits above the other." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: a student's height is typed in metres, $1.62$, while everyone else's is in centimetres. Where does that dot land on this plot?" options: ["Far below all the others, so it stands out as a mistake", "On the dashed line, where it belongs", "Far above all the others", "Exactly in the middle of the dots"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "On the line the height would equal the arm span. 1.62 is tiny next to about 160.", "A tiny number is a low dot, not a high one.", "The others are around 150 to 180 up; 1.62 is not near the middle."] explain: "1.62 up is almost at the bottom, far below dots at 150 or more. A plot makes a unit slip easy to spot." ``` ### One more student ### Same arm span ### Metres, not centimetres ## Practise: reading and checking ```step stage: practise insight: "Reading a height from an arm span on the plot, and comparing a pair with the line, over and over until across-then-up is automatic." tasks: - picture: { ref: armspan.yml#plain, caption: "The twelve students (made up)." } check: type: number q: "Find the student with arm span $170$ cm. What is their height, in cm?" answer: 168 tolerance: 1 feedback: - [170, "That is the arm span. The height is read up the side."] explain: "The dot at 170 across is at 168 up." - check: type: question q: "A student has arm span $158$ cm and height $156$ cm. Which is true of their dot?" options: ["Below the dashed line, as the height is less than the arm span", "Above the dashed line, as 158 is bigger", "On the dashed line", "Further right than the dot at arm span 160"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "158 is the arm span, which goes across. The height is 156, which is less than 158.", "On the line the two numbers are equal; these are 2 apart.", "158 is less than 160, so it is further left."] explain: "Height 156 is less than arm span 158, so the dot is below the line, and it sits left of the 160 dot." - check: type: number q: "Review: the heights of four students are $150$, $157$, $156$ and $163$ cm. What is their mean height, in cm?" answer: 156.5 explain: "150 + 157 + 156 + 163 = 626 and 626 ÷ 4 = 156.5." ``` ### Reading a height ### Below or above ### Review From earlier years: the mean of a few measurements. ## Make: is arm span the same as height? ```step stage: make insight: "Back to the opening question: counting how close the twelve dots are to the dashed line gives a first answer, and a careful sentence says what the plot shows and what it doesn't." tasks: - hint: ["For each dot, subtract the arm span from the height and ignore the sign.", "Differences: 2, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2, 4, 2. Count the ones that are 2 or less."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Use the twelve students (made up): arm span (across, up) as listed in the plot. For how many students is the height within $2$ cm of the arm span, above or below?" steps: - ["The differences (height − arm span) are $-2, 2, -2, 3, -2, 2, -3, 3, -2, 2, -4, 2$", "a dot's distance from the dashed line is its difference, whatever the sign"] - ["The sizes are $2, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2, 4, 2$", "ignore the sign: close to the line either way"] - ["$8$ of them are $2$ or less", "count them"] answer: "8" answerLabel: "Students within 2 cm" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["4", "Four is how many are NOT within 2 cm. Count the differences of 2 or less: eight of the twelve."] - ["12", "Four students are 3 or 4 cm apart, so not all twelve are within 2 cm."] criteria: - "I worked out height minus arm span for all twelve students." - "I counted a dot as close if the difference was 2 or less, above or below." explain: "The differences in size are 2, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2, 4, 2. Eight are 2 or less; the other four are 3 or 4." - check: type: question q: "Which sentence best answers 'Is your arm span the same as your height?' for these twelve students?" options: ["About the same: every dot is near the dashed line, with about half above and half below", "Exactly the same, because the dots are on the line", "No, because most of the dots are not on the line", "It can't be answered from a plot"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Only dots exactly on the line would be exactly the same, and none of the dots is on it.", "None is exactly on the line, but all are within 4 cm of it. That is close.", "A plot is just the way to see it: the dots show how close the two measurements are."] explain: "All twelve dots are within 4 cm of the dashed line, six above and six below. So arm span and height are about the same for these students, not exactly." ``` ### How close Work this out on paper first, then type your answer. ### The best sentence The twelve students and Tom are made up for this lesson. Your own class's measurements will differ. **Also used in** - **Science.** An experiment plots one measurement against another, such as the length of a spring against the weight on it. - **Sport.** A coach plots the height of players against how far they jump to look for a pattern. - **Next lesson.** Describing what a scatterplot shows: how the dots slope, how tightly they cluster and whether they follow a line. ```teacher summary: Students plot a dot from two measurements (first across, second up), read a dot's coordinates, and compare a dot with the line height = arm span. The context is a class's arm span and height with made-up numbers (AC9M10ST03, node 1). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can plot a dot from two measurements, putting the first across and the second up. - I can read the two numbers of a dot from a scatterplot. - I can say whether a dot is above, on or below the line where the two measurements are equal. struggle: Putting the two numbers the wrong way round, or reading a dot's height off the wrong axis. Ask 'which measurement did we name first, and which axis is that?' before: > Do the Run board yourself first. P snaps to whole numbers; the arrow buttons under the graph move it a step at a time. The one idea: one student is one dot, with the first measurement across and the second up. A scatterplot shows every pair at once, and a reference line (here height = arm span) gives something to compare each dot against. Every number is made up: Tom, the twelve students and the five on paper. Nothing here is a real class. If your class measures itself first (tape measures; the library's suggestion) use the real data in place of the twelve dots: the Make step then answers your own question. Measure to the nearest centimetre and agree how to measure an arm span (fingertip to fingertip, arms straight out). Hidden: measuring errors (a slumped arm span, shoes on). They show up as dots far from the line, which is where the next lesson goes. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands before the Run. Students who chose 'below' usually swapped the two numbers; ask them which axis arm span is on." - "Run: ask students to say 'across, then up' aloud as they drag P." - "Paper: the five-student try-one is worked on paper first, with the worked example beside them. Look for a dot placed on the line being counted as above." - "Modify: before the metres question ask 'about how many cm is a student tall?' and then 'where is 1.62 on that scale?'." stuck: - see: A student puts the bigger number across (Mia's mistake). ask: Which measurement did the question name first? Which axis is it on? fix: Label the axes on the page, then say 'across to arm span, up to height' as each dot is placed. - see: A student counts dots by whether they look close to the line, not by comparing the two numbers. ask: What is the height and what is the arm span? Which is bigger? fix: Write the two numbers beside the dot and compare them. A dot is above the line when the second number is bigger. - see: A student says two students with the same arm span make one dot. ask: Do they have the same height too? fix: One dot per student. The dots share their first number, so they sit one above the other. stretch: Draw a scatterplot on paper for any two measurements you can take in the classroom (hand span and foot length, say), then decide where a line like height = arm span could go, or whether none makes sense. support: Give a printed grid with the axes labelled and a row of pairs to plot one at a time, ticking each pair off. Mark 'across' and 'up' on the grid. leads: > Next: Describing association: how the dots slope, how tightly they cluster, and whether a straight line fits. Where it leads in class: students measure their own class (hand span against foot length, or arm span against height) and make the scatterplot in a spreadsheet or on paper. Any real class data replaces the made-up numbers. exit: q: A student has an arm span of 168 cm and a height of 171 cm. Which two numbers do you use to place the dot, and is it above or below the line height = arm span? a: Across 168, up 171. 171 is bigger than 168, so the dot is above the line. explain: > A scatterplot shows two measurements for each person at once. Each person is one dot. - Across: the first measurement (arm span here). - Up: the second measurement (height here). - A reference line such as height = arm span shows where the two numbers are equal: dots above it have the bigger second number, dots below it have the smaller. sources: - title: "Made up for this lesson: Tom, the twelve students' arm spans and heights, and the five pairs for the paper task. A real class would give its own numbers." url: https://tutorials.learningwaypoints.com/maths/data/scatterplots/ checked: 2026-10-25 ```

# Boards for "Scatterplots". Made-up measurements for a class of 12: arm span across (x), height up (y), in cm.
# The dashed line is height = arm span. P is a dot students drag to plot one more student.

# region: run
widget: graph
axes: Arm span (cm), Height (cm)
x: 140, 190
y: 140, 190
grid: 10
snap: 1
plot: y = x, dashed
series Class: 152,150; 155,157; 158,156; 160,163; 162,160; 164,166; 166,163; 168,171; 170,168; 173,175; 176,172; 181,183, dots
point P: 165, 165, drag
# endregion

# region: plain

axes: Arm span (cm), Height (cm)
x: 140, 190
y: 140, 190
grid: 10
plot: y = x, dashed

# endregion

# Mia's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: mia
Tom has an arm span of 150 cm and a height of 175 cm.
The axes are arm span across the bottom and height up the side.
I start at the corner and go across to 175, because 175 is the bigger number.
Then I go up to 150 and put my dot there.
That dot is below the dashed line, so Tom's arm span is longer than his height.
# endregion
